title: Founding Infosys with $250 borrowed from his wife
statement: Murthy and six co-founders started Infosys with Rs 10,000 — roughly $250, borrowed from his wife Sudha — after his earlier venture and a communist-phase arrest had failed, betting on exporting Indian software talent.
outcome: Infosys became the bellwether of Indian IT services, grew to employ hundreds of thousands, and its 1999 NASDAQ listing — the first Indian company listed there — created the outsourcing era's flagship.

title: The Global Delivery Model — shipping work, not people
statement: Infosys pioneered the offshore development center model — doing client work from India at a fraction of on-site cost — codified as the Global Delivery Model.
outcome: The GDM became the industry standard, created the Indian IT services sector, and enabled the cost-quality positioning that made the sector globally competitive.

title: Voluntary delisting fight and transparency-first governance
statement: When the 1990s buyback boom tempted the founders to cash out, Murthy refused to buy back shares below fair value, insisting that minority shareholders' interests were the company's highest obligation.
outcome: The governance reputation enabled the 1999 ADR listing at a premium and made Infosys the West's trusted counterpart for Indian delivery; Murthy became the global face of Indian corporate integrity.

title: ESOPs — making thousands of employees rupee millionaires
statement: Infosys was among the first Indian companies to distribute stock options broadly across its engineering workforce, aligning employees with the listing.
outcome: Widely-distributed ESOP wealth created Bangalore's first generation of professional wealth and became a talent weapon the rest of the industry was forced to copy.
